# Abstract

Between the proclamation of Dominion status on 26 September 1907 and the close of the first quarter of the twenty-first century, Aotearoa New Zealand nearly quintupled in population while undergoing a profound geographic and ethnic realignment [@pool2026peopling; @aotearoa20242023]. Across sixteen modern Regional Councils and the Chatham Islands Territory covering 304.565,6 km² of buffered coastal and island mask footprint (269.400 km² of subaerial Historical GIS land area), national headcounts climbed from 1,05M at the 1911 Dominion census (1.008.468 non-Māori enumerated alongside roughly 49,8k Māori) to 1,94M in 1951, 3,38M in 1991, 4,03M in 2006 and 4,99M (4.993.926, density 16,4 inhabitants per km²) at the 2023 Census, before surpassing 5,1M on the 2025 decadal raster and roughly 5,3M in official resident estimates [@statistics1962population; @aotearoa20242023; @crothers2021research]. Despite heavy young-male losses in the First World War and roughly 9k deaths during the 1918 influenza pandemic, sustained post-war fertility, rapid Māori demographic recovery and successive waves of British, Pacific and post-1987 Asian skilled migration drove compound growth averaging 1,4% per annum across 1911 to 2023 [@pool1991iwi; @spoonley2012welcome]. Spatially, the dominant twentieth-century current was the relentless North Island demographic drift: the North Island rose from 55,9% of non-Māori residents in 1911 (62,3% of total population in 1921) to 67,7% in 1951, 74,6% in 1991 and 76,3% (3,81M) in 2023, powered by Auckland Region's ascent to 1,66M inhabitants (33,2% of the nation; density 200,49 per km²) under its 2010 unified municipal council boundary [@jackson2019subnational; @alimi2019more]. In the South Island (1,19M, 23,7%), Canterbury (651k) absorbed post-2010 earthquake suburbanisation across Selwyn and Waimakariri while alpine tourism revived central Otago and rural peripheral districts aged rapidly [@whitehead2023comparison]. Across 547 catalogued urban and rural settlements and 2.527 dated observations, the six Official Functional Urban Areas hold 3,06M people (61,3% of New Zealand), yielding a steep primate rank-size slope ($\alpha = 1,23$, $R^2 = 0,98$ across the top 180 centres) anchored by metropolitan Auckland (1,62M), Christchurch (510,8k) and Wellington (418,2k).

# Background

## Dominion Status, First World War Losses and the Interwar Drift (1907 to 1945)

When New Zealand transitioned from self-governing colony to the Dominion of New Zealand on 26 September 1907, its population had just crossed the one-million threshold and was entering a century of rapid modernisation [@pool2026peopling; @pool2007new]. The 1911 census recorded 1.008.468 non-Māori residents alongside 49.844 persons counted on a separate Māori roll, yielding a benchmark total of 1,05M across the archipelago. Refrigerated shipping had already shifted export momentum away from South Island wool and gold toward North Island dairying and frozen meat across Waikato, Taranaki, Manawatū and the Bay of Plenty [@pool2026peopling]. Where the South Island had held a clear colonial majority in the 1880s, by 1911 the North Island provincial districts already contained 55,9% of New Zealand's non-Māori inhabitants (563.733 against 444.735 in the South Island) and over 95% of the Māori population.

Two abrupt demographic shocks scarred the Dominion's opening decade. Between 1914 and 1918, New Zealand mobilised roughly 100k personnel for overseas service in the First World War—nearly a tenth of the entire national population—suffering roughly 18k military fatalities concentrated heavily among young men aged twenty to thirty-four [@pool2007new]. Before demobilisation had finished, the November 1918 H1N1 influenza pandemic swept the country in six weeks, killing roughly 9k people; Māori communities suffered death rates roughly seven times higher than those of European New Zealanders, temporarily checking the fragile post-1896 Māori demographic recovery [@pool1991iwi; @pool2026peopling]. Together, war casualties and influenza depressed intercensal growth between 1911 and 1921 while creating a lasting deficit of young adult men across rural counties and small boroughs.

Even so, assisted British immigration and buoyant pastoral exports lifted total population including Māori to 1.271.664 in 1921, 1.347.853 in 1924 and 1.573.810 at the delayed 1936 census [@dixon1989new]. The Great Depression of 1929 to 1935 sharply curtailed overseas migration—actually turning net arrivals negative in the early 1930s—and pushed non-Māori total fertility down to a historic interwar trough near replacement level, forcing the government to cancel the scheduled 1931 census for fiscal economy [@dixon1989new; @pool2007new]. By 1936, the North Island share had climbed to 64,7% (1.018.036 residents), led by Auckland Province (546.970) and Wellington Province (316.446), while South Island growth slowed to a crawl outside Christchurch (133,5k metropolitan area in 1936) and Dunedin (85,6k). The Second World War again drew over 140k New Zealanders into military service, cost nearly 12k lives and delayed the scheduled 1941 enumeration until September 1945, when national population stood at 1.702.298 [@dixon1989new; @pool2026peopling].

## Post-War Baby Boom, Māori Urban Migration and Resurgence (1945 to 1984)

The three decades following 1945 delivered the fastest sustained natural increase in twentieth-century New Zealand history [@pool2007new; @pool2026peopling]. Full employment, state housing construction, universal family benefits and early near-universal marriage drove non-Māori total fertility above 4 births per woman by 1961, while assisted British and Dutch immigration replenished industrial and agricultural labour [@spoonley2012welcome; @pool2007new]. Total census population rose from 1.939.472 in 1951 to 2.414.984 in 1961 (+2,22% per annum), 2.862.631 in 1971 and 3.130.083 in 1976 [@statistics1962population]. Simultaneously, the geographic centre of gravity kept marching north: North Island statistical areas reached 69,8% of national population in 1961 (1.684.785) and 72,5% in 1976 (2.268.344), as Central Auckland (514.507 to 798.291) and South Auckland–Bay of Plenty (349.624 to 471.665) outpaced every southern province [@statistics1962population].

Within this post-war expansion unfolded one of the fastest indigenous urban transitions recorded anywhere in the modern world [@pool1991iwi; @kukutai2011contemporary]. At the 1945 census, roughly three quarters of Māori still lived in rural districts across Northland, the East Coast, Bay of Plenty, Waikato and the central North Island. Rapid Māori demographic resurgence—combining plummeting infant and infectious-disease mortality with sustained high fertility—created large cohorts of young Māori entering adulthood just as mechanised farming shrank rural employment and urban factories, freezing works, forestry mills and railways sought workers [@pool1991iwi; @rarere2019understandin]. Within a single generation between 1945 and 1981, over three quarters of Māori relocated to cities and towns, concentrating in South and West Auckland, Porirua, Lower Hutt, Hamilton, Rotorua and purpose-built forestry hubs such as Tokoroa (18,7k at its 1981 peak) [@pool1991iwi; @kukutai2011contemporary]. Even as overall New Zealand fertility fell below replacement after 1978, Māori fertility remained distinctly above non-Māori levels across the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries, sustaining a markedly younger Māori age pyramid and lifting the Māori ethnic share toward a sixth of the national total [@rarere2019understandin; @rarere2024understandin; @urale2019relationship].

Parallel labour migration transformed New Zealand into a central hub of the Polynesian Pacific [@spoonley2012welcome; @kingstone1990brief]. From the late 1950s through the mid-1970s, manufacturing growth in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch attracted tens of thousands of migrants from Sāmoa, the Cook Islands, Niue, Tokelau, Tonga and Fiji—including New Zealand citizens from the Realm territories of Cook Islands, Niue and Tokelau [@spoonley2012welcome]. Although the 1973 oil shock and Britain's entry into the European Economic Community triggered economic contraction, heavy net emigration to Australia and restrictive policing of Pacific overstayers during the mid-1970s, New Zealand-born Pacific cohorts and sustained family reunification anchored large, youthful Pacific communities in Auckland and Wellington [@kingstone1990brief; @urale2019relationship; @spoonley2012welcome].

## Economic Restructuring, Post-1987 Skilled Migration and Twenty-First-Century Shocks (1984 to 2026)

From 1984 onward, radical economic deregulation dismantled agricultural subsidies, tariff walls and state-owned industrial enterprises, triggering severe job losses in freezing works, timber towns, railways and provincial manufacturing [@blakely2008inequalities; @hancock2015where]. Rural regions such as Southland, Taranaki, Gisborne, West Coast and inland Manawatū stagnated or lost working-age residents while professional, financial and service employment consolidated in Auckland and Wellington [@hancock2015where; @jackson2019subnational]. Cohort mortality studies covering the 1981 to 2004 censuses demonstrate that this economic restructuring coincided with a sharp widening of socioeconomic and ethnic mortality inequalities, as Māori and Pacific workers absorbed disproportionate unemployment while European mortality continued falling [@blakely2008inequalities; @disney2017changing].

Three years into economic reform, the Immigration Act 1987 abolished New Zealand's historic preference for British and European source countries, replacing origin quotas with skills, capital and points-based selection [@spoonley2012welcome]. The demographic consequences were immediate and cumulative. Large inflows from East, South and Southeast Asia—particularly China, India, the Philippines, South Korea and Malaysia—alongside continuing British, South African and Pacific migration propelled Auckland into one of the most ethnically diverse port metropolises in the OECD [@spoonley2012welcome; @kanengoni2018setting; @montayre2017moving]. Immigrant cohorts aged into New Zealand's urban fabric alongside New Zealand-born generations, prompting new policy attention to migrant health trajectories, transnational family caregiving and older Asian settlement adjustment [@kanengoni2018setting; @montayre2017moving]. Between 1991 and 2023, Auckland Region alone added 712.710 inhabitants—growing from 943.776 (27,9% of New Zealand) to 1.656.486 (33,2%)—accounting for 44,1% of total national population growth over thirty-two years [@aotearoa20242023].

To align urban governance with this expanding metropolitan footprint, Parliament enacted the Local Government (Auckland Council) reorganisation effective 1 November 2010, merging seven territorial councils (Auckland City, Manukau, Waitākere, North Shore, Papakura, Rodney and most of Franklin) with the Auckland Regional Council into a single unitary Auckland Council retaining unified regional-municipal limits [@alimi2019more; @jackson2019subnational]. Across the South Island, a seismic shock reshaped Canterbury just months later: the September 2010 Darfield (Mw 7,1) and February 2011 Christchurch (Mw 6,2) earthquakes killed 185 people, demolished much of central Christchurch, red-zoned thousands of eastern suburban homes and deferred the 2011 national census until March 2013 [@aotearoa20202018]. Rather than depopulating Canterbury, earthquake reconstruction redirected tens of thousands of households into outer plains commuters in Selwyn District (where Rolleston surged more than fivefold from 5.022 in 2006 to 28.449 in 2023, and Lincoln nearly quadrupled from 2.820 to 10.611) and Waimakariri District (Rangiora rising from 12,2k to 18,9k and Kaiapoi from 10,6k to 13k).

Finally, the 2020 to 2022 COVID-19 pandemic produced a unique demographic pause and rebound. Strict maritime and aviation border closures halted international arrivals for nearly two years while preventing mass pandemic mortality; Bayesian excess-mortality modelling confirms that New Zealand experienced negative excess mortality during 2020–2021 and markedly lower cumulative pandemic mortality than peer OECD states once Omicron arrived in 2022, informed closely by empirical household age-contact structures [@bryant2026estimating; @sullivan2024quantifying]. Reopening borders in mid-2022 unleashed a record temporary surge of skilled, student and working-holiday arrivals alongside elevated trans-Tasman departures, lifting the March 2023 Census usually resident count to 4.993.926 (+6,3% above 2018) and propelling estimated resident population past 5,3M by 2025 [@aotearoa20242023; @crothers2021research].

## Mortality Transition, Ethnic Differentials and Structural Ageing

Long-run twentieth-century gains lifted New Zealand life expectancy at birth past 80 years for men and 83 years for women, placing Aotearoa near the global longevity frontier alongside Australia [@ryan2024differences; @pool2026peopling]. Yet linked national census-mortality cohorts spanning 68,9M person-years between 1981 and 2011 reveal enduring, if shifting, ethnic and socioeconomic mortality gradients [@disney2017changing]. Cardiovascular, respiratory and cancer mortality fell across all populations, yet Māori and Pacific life expectancy still trailed European and Asian benchmarks by roughly six to seven years in the early 2020s—driven heavily by tobacco-attributable mortality, metabolic and diabetic disease burdens and inequitable access to specialist clinical care [@sandiford2013application; @versterf2026life; @white2026decreasing; @ryan2024differences].

Concurrently, sustained sub-replacement fertility among European and Asian New Zealanders has accelerated subnational demographic ageing [@jackson2019subnational; @crothers2021research]. While youthful Māori, Pacific and immigrant cohorts keep Auckland, Hamilton and Wellington structurally younger, rural and coastal districts across Northland, Thames-Coromandel, Whanganui, Kāpiti Coast, Marlborough, Nelson, Tasman, West Coast and Southland face rapidly rising pensioner shares and shrinking working-age bases—reshaping regional income inequality and health-service demand across the urban-rural divide [@jackson2019subnational; @alimi2019more; @whitehead2023comparison].

# Methodology

## Seventeen-Unit Regional Council Partition and Administrative Evolution

To maintain constant-boundary spatial comparability across 1907 to 2026, AUSTRAL partitions modern New Zealand into seventeen administrative sub-regions corresponding to the sixteen statutory Regional Councils established under the Local Government Amendment Act 1989 plus the special-purpose Chatham Islands Territory. Together, these seventeen units occupy 304.565,6 km² of buffered coastal and island mask footprint (269.400 km² of subaerial Historical GIS land area). Nine regions comprise the North Island (133.483,8 km² mask area: Northland, Auckland, Waikato, Bay of Plenty, Gisborne, Hawke's Bay, Taranaki, Manawatu-Wanganui and Wellington), seven comprise the South Island (168.486 km²: West Coast, Canterbury, Otago, Southland, Tasman, Nelson and Marlborough) and the Chatham Islands Territory (2.595,8 km² buffered marine-island mask around Rēkohu/Wharekauri and Pitt Island) sits roughly 800 km east of Christchurch.

Modern New Zealand underwent four successive subnational statistical boundary regimes after 1907, creating a classic modifiable-areal-unit challenge for longitudinal demography [@dixon1989new; @statistics1962population]. From 1907 through 1951, the Department of Statistics published census returns by ten Provincial Districts (separating the Otago and Southland portions of Otago Province, plus offshore territories—eleven polygons spanning 263.668 km² in our HGIS archive), where a single vast Auckland Province (59.486 km²) combined modern Northland, Auckland, Waikato, Bay of Plenty and Gisborne. Between 1961 and 1976, Stats NZ shifted to thirteen Statistical Areas that split Central Auckland from Northland, South Auckland–Bay of Plenty and East Coast [@statistics1962population]. Between 1981 and 1986, censuses reported twenty-two Local Government Regions, before the 1989 reorganisation established the sixteen Regional Councils (with minor 1992 adjustments separating Tasman, Nelson and Marlborough) and the 2010 Auckland Council Act unified metropolitan Auckland's territorial and regional jurisdictions under identical external limits. Our dataset pairs the constant-boundary seventeen-region benchmark matrix (1911, 1951, 1991, 2006 and 2023) with a 135-row Historical GIS territorial regime panel (1910 to 2025) and the original official provincial and statistical-area census enumerations (1911 to 1981) so shifting boundaries remain fully visible.

## Five-Yearly Censuses, Ethnic Enumeration and Growth Metrics

New Zealand's modern statistical record rests on one of the longest unbroken quinquennial census series in the world—conducted every five years from 1906 through 2023, interrupted only by Depression cancellation in 1931, wartime deferral from 1941 to 1945 and the Canterbury earthquake postponement from 2011 to 2013 [@dixon1989new; @aotearoa20202018; @aotearoa20242023]. Technically, three enumeration shifts govern long-run interpretation. First, Māori were enumerated on separate schedules until 1951 and excluded from early provincial summary tables such as the 1911 non-Māori provincial breakdown (1.008.468), requiring careful addition of the concurrent Māori roll (49.844) for full national totals [@dixon1989new; @pool1991iwi]. Second, Stats NZ replaced biological blood-quantum definitions with self-identified cultural ethnicity from 1986 onward and abandoned single-category ethnic prioritisation in favour of multi-response totals in 2004, a methodological shift with major implications for Māori, Pacific and mixed-heritage trend analysis [@didham2012effect; @kukutai2011contemporary]. Third, after the digital-first 2018 Census suffered an acute response drop among Māori and Pacific households—necessitating unprecedented administrative-data imputation from the Integrated Data Infrastructure—Stats NZ redesigned field collection for March 2023, overcoming Cyclone Gabrielle disruptions across Northland, Gisborne and Hawke's Bay to publish official usually resident counts reaching 4.993.926 [@kukutai2019census; @aotearoa20202018; @aotearoa20242023].

For every regional unit $r$ across benchmark or census horizons $t_1$ and $t_2$, national totals $P_{\text{NZ}}(t)$, North Island population shares $S_{\text{NI}}(t)$ and compound annual growth rates $g_r(t_1, t_2)$ are computed uniformly across harmonised counts:

$$P_{\text{NZ}}(t) = \sum_{r=1}^{17} P_r(t), \qquad S_{\text{NI}}(t) = \frac{\sum_{r \in \text{NI}} P_r(t)}{P_{\text{NZ}}(t)}$$

$$g_r(t_1, t_2) = \left(\frac{P_r(t_2)}{P_r(t_1)}\right)^{\frac{1}{t_2 - t_1}} - 1$$

Because the sixteen Regional Councils did not exist prior to 1989, the constant-boundary benchmark series backcasts 1911 and 1951 Regional Council cells proportionally from the 1991 Regional Council distribution to national totals, whereas the primary provincial and statistical-area enumerations (1911, 1921, 1936, 1945, 1951, 1961, 1971, 1976 and 1981) and the twenty-slice raster panel (1910 to 2025) supply the historical inter-island and provincial shift directly. Both series are presented side by side below.

## Four-Wave Settlement Gazetteer Assembly and Functional Urban Areas

Alongside regional totals, AUSTRAL compiles an evidence-based settlement gazetteer documenting 547 urban and rural localities and 2.527 dated census observations (mean 4,62 benchmarks per settlement) across 1911 to 2023. Every record derives strictly from official Stats NZ primary archives—namely the 2006, 2013, 2018 and 2023 Statistical Area 2 (SA2) and Urban-Rural 2023 census series (536 localities), the Stats NZ Historical County and Borough Populations 1891–1996 series (89 long-running boroughs), the Official Functional Urban Areas 2023 metropolitan aggregation (6 major metropolises) and the New Zealand Official Yearbook 2002 historical urban tables (6 metropolises)—achieving 0% crowd-sourced fallback across all seventeen regions.

Gazetteer assembly proceeded through four audited source-ledger waves. Wave 1 ingested all 547 primary official census localities and historical borough time series. Wave 2 cross-checked peer-reviewed historical demography without injecting synthetic figures. Wave 3 executed municipal reconciliation and deduplication, excluding 71 non-canonical candidate records: 67 Territorial Authority district aggregates (superseded by individual urban and rural settlement localities to prevent rural-county double counting) and 4 duplicate coastal locality aliases merged within 25 km of their canonical settlements (Pārua Bay into Whangārei Heads, Glenbrook Beach into Clarks Beach, Plummers Point into Te Puna West and Rainbows End into Sandspit). Wave 4 ran a targeted sub-region coverage sweep closing with 2 final verification records (0,37% marginal gain, well beneath the 2% saturation ceiling), 0 empty sub-regions and 0 unaccounted candidates. Spatial scope cleanly distinguishes 6 metropolitan Functional Urban Areas (Auckland, Christchurch, Wellington, Hamilton, Tauranga and Dunedin), 55 suburban commuter towns and 486 city-proper urban and rural centres.

# Testing and Validation

## Reconciliation Across Provincial, Statistical-Area, HGIS and Regional Council Series

Reconciling our twenty-slice decadal/quinquennial raster totals against the 135-row Historical GIS territorial regime panel across nine shared benchmark years (1910 to 2025) confirms near-exact numerical convergence across every modern regime. From 1960 onward—when the HGIS layer switches from eleven historical provinces (263.668 km²) to the seventeen modern Regional Council polygons (269.400 km²)—agreement reaches 0% rounding precision: 2.296.061 HGIS against 2.296.060 raster in 1960, 3.069.519 against 3.069.518 in 1980, 3.713.255 against 3.713.253 in 2000, 4.149.637 against 4.149.636 in 2010, 4.815.074 against 4.815.076 in 2020 and an identical 5.103.793 in 2025. Across the three pre-1955 provincial HGIS snapshots, modest deficits of -1,35% in 1910 (990.976 HGIS against 1.004.564 raster), -1,24% in 1920 (1.242.945 against 1.258.564) and -2,65% in 1950 (1.898.178 against 1.949.910) reflect small differences in offshore-island inclusion, coastal shipping crews and intercensal interpolation between 1911/1921/1951 census nights and decadal round dates.

Three structural modelling artefacts appear when comparing the constant-boundary 17-region benchmark table, the 20-slice raster panel and the primary historical census tables, and each warrants explicit disclosure. First, because the 17-unit benchmark matrix backcasts 1911 and 1951 values proportionally from 1991 Regional Council shares, it holds the North Island benchmark share flat at 74,6% across 1911, 1951 and 1991 (27,9% for Auckland Region) rather than displaying the true twentieth-century northward shift (55,9% non-Māori in 1911, 62,3% total in 1921, 67,7% in 1951, 69,8% in 1961 and 72,5% in 1976) documented in Table \ref{tab:census-series}. Second, inside the decadal raster panel, uniform areal disaggregation of the old eleven-province geometry across 1910 to 1940 temporarily spreads Auckland Province's population evenly over Northland, Waikato, Bay of Plenty and Gisborne—under-allocating compact Auckland Region (31,1k to 59k in 1910–1940) until the 1955 transition snaps Auckland to its true urban concentration (575,9k in 1955, 634,8k in 1960 and 1,67M in 2025); similarly, a minor 2020–2025 border-pixel trade-off shifts roughly 31k people from compact Nelson (904,6 km²) into adjoining Tasman on the coarse raster while preserving their combined top-of-the-South total (105,9k raster in 2020 against 110,4k census in 2023), and Chatham Islands' constant-boundary 1991/2006 placeholder (5.000) resolves cleanly to the true 2023 census count of 633 (654 raster in 2020; 647 in 2025). Third, excluding all 67 Territorial Authority district aggregates from the 547-settlement locality gazetteer prevents double counting of rural districts but also removes several mid-sized provincial cities whose official boundary matched a Territorial Authority (Whangārei, Gisborne, Napier, Hastings, New Plymouth, Palmerston North, Whanganui, Nelson, Timaru and Invercargill), while the Otago borough of Palmerston carries a 1911 archival homonym value (10.991, matching 1911 Palmerston North) before returning to its true village scale (868 in 1961; 1.056 in 2023).

## Census Coverage Diagnostics and Ethnic Classification Consistency

Independent demographic evaluations confirm generally high enumeration completeness across New Zealand's modern censuses while pinpointing well-known modern error margins [@dixon1989new; @kukutai2019census; @aotearoa20242023]. Post-enumeration surveys from 1996 through 2013 recorded net national undercount around 1,2% to 2,4%, skewed toward young adult males, highly mobile urban renters, Māori and Pacific peoples. In 2018, an abrupt shift to an online-first operating model caused individual response rates to fall sharply—down to roughly 68% for Māori and 65% for Pacific peoples—forcing Stats NZ to incorporate administrative tax, health and education records for over 11% of the usually resident count [@kukutai2019census; @aotearoa20202018]. Tahu Kukutai and Donna Cormack demonstrated that administrative imputation salvaged national headcounts while weakening iwi-affiliation reliability and local Māori planning data [@kukutai2019census]. Improved field outreach in 2023 restored direct collection across most of the country, though Cyclone Gabrielle required extended enumeration across Tairāwhiti/Gisborne and Hawke's Bay [@aotearoa20242023]. Furthermore, Robert Didham and Paul Callister showed that switching between prioritised and total-response ethnicity materially alters ethnic denominators in health and fertility analysis [@didham2012effect], while Jesse Whitehead and colleagues confirmed that applying the Geographic Classification for Health to 2018 Census data reveals substantially sharper rural socioeconomic and Māori population disparities than older urban-rural binary thresholds [@whitehead2023comparison].

# Results

## National Demographic Trajectory (1907 to 2026)

New Zealand's modern demographic expansion divides into four distinct waves visible across Figure \ref{fig:nz-trajectory}: steady Dominion pastoral growth dampened by war and depression (1907 to 1945), the rapid post-war baby boom (1945 to 1976), late-century deceleration during economic restructuring and trans-Tasman outflow (1976 to 1991) and immigration-led metropolitan resurgence across the early twenty-first century (1991 to 2026) [@pool2026peopling; @spoonley2012welcome; @crothers2021research]. Starting from 1M on the 1910 decadal raster (1,05M at the 1911 census benchmark), national numbers reached 1,26M in 1920 (1,27M at the 1921 census), 1,47M in 1930, 1,65M in 1940 (1,7M in 1945) and 1,95M in 1950 (1,94M at the 1951 census). Across the thirty post-war years from 1945 to 1976, New Zealand added 1,43M people—nearly doubling inside three decades—to pass two million in 1952 and three million in 1973 (3,13M at the 1976 census) [@statistics1962population; @pool2007new].

<figure class="crd-figure-block" id="fig:nz-trajectory">
<img class="crd-figure-img" src="/artefacts/project_austral/1.0-modern-new-zealand/modern_new_zealand_population_trajectory.png" alt="fig:nz-trajectory" loading="lazy" />
<figcaption class="crd-caption"><span class="crd-caption-label">Figure 2.</span> Modern New Zealand population trajectory from 1907 to 2023 across leading Regional Councils (Panel A) and 2023 regional population density rankings across the ten most densely peopled regions (Panel B).</figcaption>
</figure>

Growth cooled sharply between 1976 and 1991 as falling fertility collided with cyclical emigration to Australia, lifting total population by only 248k over fifteen years (+0,51% per annum) to 3.378.191 in 1991 [@pool2026peopling; @blakely2008inequalities]. Post-1987 skilled immigration then re-ignited national expansion: New Zealand crossed four million in 2003 (4.034.501 at the 2006 census, +1,19% per annum across 1991–2006) and added nearly one million more residents over the next seventeen years to reach 4.993.926 at the March 2023 Census (+1,26% per annum across 2006–2023), before climbing to 5,1M on the 2025 raster and roughly 5,3M in official mid-2025 resident population estimates [@aotearoa20242023; @crothers2021research]. Across the entire 112-year census interval from 1911 to 2023, Aotearoa New Zealand expanded 4,77-fold (+1,4% per annum), raising national mean density from 3,44 to 16,4 inhabitants per km² across the buffered archipelago footprint (18,54 per km² on strict subaerial HGIS land area).

Table \ref{tab:census-series} tracks official Stats NZ provincial enumerations across five landmark censuses from 1911 to 1951, documenting the relentless southward-to-northward inversion during the Dominion half-century. Whereas Canterbury (173,4k), Otago (132,4k) and Southland (58,7k) still accounted for more than a third of non-Māori New Zealand in 1911, Auckland Province nearly tripled in forty years from 264,5k (non-Māori) in 1911 to 745,1k (total) in 1951—exceeding the entire South Island (625,6k) by almost 120k people [@statistics1962population].

## Upper North Island Core: Auckland, Waikato, Bay of Plenty and Northland

By 2023, the four northernmost Regional Councils—Auckland, Waikato, Bay of Plenty and Northland—contained 2.683.404 inhabitants, or 53,7% of all New Zealanders on just 23,1% of the national mask footprint (70.510,3 km²) [@aotearoa20242023]. Together, Auckland, Hamilton and Tauranga form the urban "Golden Triangle" that now dominates national manufacturing, logistics, tertiary education and international migration [@jackson2019subnational; @alimi2019more].

Auckland Region (8.262,4 km²) stands in a demographic class of its own. From a modest colonial seaport of 102,7k in 1911, Auckland Metro multiplied more than fifteenfold across the twentieth and early twenty-first centuries—reaching 226,4k in 1936, 448,4k in 1961, 878,2k in 1991, 1,28M in 2006 and 1.622.925 in 2023 within a wider Auckland Region of 1.656.486 (33,2% of New Zealand; density 200,49 inhabitants per km², twelve times the national mean) [@aotearoa20242023]. Post-war Māori and Pacific urban settlement concentrated across South and West Auckland, followed after 1987 by large Chinese, Indian, Filipino and Korean communities across Central, East and North Shore suburbs—making Auckland the world's largest Polynesian city and New Zealand's primary immigrant gateway [@spoonley2012welcome; @kanengoni2018setting; @montayre2017moving]. Unified since November 2010 under the single Auckland Council boundary, growth now radiates both north along the Hibiscus Coast (36,9k in 2006 to 63,4k in 2023) and Warkworth (6,5k) and south across Pukekohe (1,5k in 1916 to 27k in 2023), Waiuku (9,5k), Beachlands-Pine Harbour (7,8k) and cross-border Pōkeno (1,8k in 2006 to 7,8k in 2023), alongside island suburbs at Waiheke West (6,8k).

Directly south, Waikato Region (29.899,3 km²) climbed from 331.026 in 1991 to 380.823 in 2006 and 498.771 in 2023 (10% of New Zealand; density 16,68 per km²), emerging as the country's fourth-largest region. Intensive dairying, Auckland commuter spillover along the Waikato Expressway and rapid university-city expansion propelled Hamilton Metro sixtyfold from 3.543 in 1911 to 50.505 in 1961, 146.148 in 1991 and 213.933 in 2023. Prosperous market and commuting satellites ring the basin—Cambridge (1,5k in 1911 to 21,4k in 2023), Te Awamutu (13,4k), Matamata (9,1k), Morrinsville (9k), Huntly (8,2k), Ngāruawāhia (8k) and historic gold town Waihī (6,4k in 1911, dipping to 3,2k in 1961 before reviving to 8,1k in 2023)—contrasting sharply with forestry-dependent Tokoroa, which surged to 18.713 in 1981 before timber-mill restructuring pared it back to 12,3k in 2013 and 14k in 2023.

Bay of Plenty Region (14.724,2 km²) posted the briskest proportional expansion outside Auckland over the past three decades, rising 63,8% from 203.982 in 1991 to 257.358 in 2006 and 334.140 in 2023 (6,7% of New Zealand; density 22,69 per km², fourth highest nationally). Export container shipping at Port of Tauranga, kiwifruit horticulture and retiree inflows lifted Tauranga Metro an astonishing 127-fold from 1.347 in 1911 to 24.660 in 1961, 70.257 in 1991 and 171.105 in 2023, absorbing former Mount Maunganui Borough (12,4k in 1986) and lifting nearby horticultural hubs such as Te Puke (9,1k in 2023) and Ōmokoroa (5,8k). North of Auckland, Northland Region (17.624,4 km²) grew steadily from 126.786 in 1991 to 148.470 in 2006 and 194.007 in 2023 (3,9% of New Zealand; density 11,01 per km²), combining a large, resilient rural and small-town Māori population across the Far North with brisk coastal lifestyle growth in Kerikeri (5,5k in 2006 to 8,1k in 2023), Mangawhai Heads (2,9k) and Waipū [@rarere2024understandin; @whitehead2023comparison].

## Lower and Eastern North Island: Wellington, Manawatu-Wanganui, Hawke's Bay, Taranaki and Gisborne

Across the southern and eastern North Island, five regions held 1.124.607 inhabitants in 2023 (22,5% of New Zealand), displaying a sharp divide between the dense national capital belt and slower-growing pastoral provinces [@jackson2019subnational]. Wellington Region (9.181 km²) grew from 400.284 in 1991 to 448.752 in 2006 and 520.971 in 2023 (10,4% of New Zealand; density 56,74 per km², third highest nationally). As New Zealand's political, public-service and cultural capital, Wellington Metro expanded nearly sixfold from 70.728 in 1911 to 249.531 in 1961, 324.156 in 1991 and 418.152 in 2023, spanning steep harbour hills, the Hutt Valley industrial corridor and Porirua's large Māori and Pacific communities before spilling north up the Kāpiti Coast to Paraparaumu (28,9k in 2023; 30,1k in 2020) and Waikanae (13k) and east over the Remutaka Range into Wairarapa commuting towns such as Carterton (5,8k) and Featherston (2,9k). Notably, Christchurch overtook Wellington as New Zealand's second-largest Functional Urban Area by 2006 (407,6k against 366,9k) and widened that lead to 92,6k residents by 2023.

Manawatu-Wanganui Region (20.558,6 km²) stagnated during the 1990s restructuring (224.760 in 1991 to 222.642 in 2006) before recovering to 251.412 in 2023 (5% of New Zealand; density 12,23 per km²), supported by tertiary education, defence and logistics around Palmerston North alongside steady towns at Levin (1,6k in 1911 to 19,5k in 2023), Feilding (3,2k to 16,9k), Marton (5,5k), Dannevirke (5,5k) and Taumarunui (4,8k, down from its 6,5k 1981 forestry-railway peak). Along the eastern coast, Hawke's Bay Region (15.243,5 km²) expanded from 138.342 in 1991 to 175.074 in 2023 (3,5% of New Zealand; density 11,49 per km²), led by the twin Napier–Hastings urban plain and affluent orchard suburb Havelock North (2,6k in 1956 to 15k in 2023), though devastated locally by Cyclone Gabrielle in February 2023. On the western volcanic cone, dairy and offshore oil-and-gas hub Taranaki Region (8.897,2 km²) dipped from 107.127 in 1991 to 104.127 in 2006 before rebounding to 126.015 in 2023 (2,5%; density 14,16 per km²), backed by Hāwera (2,7k in 1911 to 10,4k in 2023), Waitara (7,5k) and Stratford (6,2k). At the northeastern edge, Gisborne Region (9.093,2 km²) recorded New Zealand's highest regional Māori population share (exceeding half of residents) alongside slow aggregate growth (44.265 in 1991, 44.436 in 2006 and 51.135 in 2023; 1% of the nation; density 5,62 per km²) [@aotearoa20242023; @rarere2024understandin].

## South Island and the Chatham Islands: Canterbury, Otago, Southland, Top of the South and West Coast

Home to 1.185.282 inhabitants in 2023 (23,7% of New Zealand on 55,3% of its buffered land footprint), the South Island reflects stark internal contrasts between booming Canterbury and Central Otago and slowly growing or stagnant peripheral coasts [@jackson2019subnational; @whitehead2023comparison]. Canterbury Region (48.444 km², New Zealand's largest region by area) anchors 54,9% of the South Island's entire population, expanding 48,6% from 438.171 in 1991 to 521.835 in 2006 and 651.027 in 2023 (13% of New Zealand; density 13,44 per km²). Christchurch Metro grew from 80.193 in 1911 to 220.509 in 1961, 303.411 in 1991 and 407.610 in 2006; after the 2010–2011 earthquakes briefly slowed metropolitan growth (414.258 in 2013), massive reconstruction, Asian and British skilled immigration and greenfield suburban migration lifted the Functional Urban Area by nearly 100k residents in a decade to 510.801 in 2023 [@aotearoa20242023]. That post-quake outward dispersal transformed outer plains satellites into boom towns: Rolleston rocketed from 5.022 in 2006 to 28.449 in 2023 (+10,7% per annum), Rangiora jumped from 12,2k to 18,9k, Kaiapoi rose from 10,6k to 13k, Lincoln climbed from 2,8k to 10,6k and Prebbleton doubled past 5,6k.

Otago Region (32.584,1 km²) illustrates a dual demographic economy, climbing from 177.525 in 1991 to 193.854 in 2006 and 240.900 in 2023 (4,8% of New Zealand; density 7,39 per km²). Once New Zealand's richest Victorian city, coastal Dunedin Metro grew modestly over a century—from 64.236 in 1911 to 105.003 in 1961, 107.523 in 1991 and 124.839 in 2023—anchored by the University of Otago and satellite Mosgiel (1,6k in 1911 to 14,6k in 2023) alongside coastal Oamaru (13,7k). Inland, by contrast, global alpine tourism and amenity migration turned former goldfields into New Zealand's fastest-growing interior corridor: Queenstown jumped thirty-fivefold from 696 in 1911 and 1.321 in 1961 to 11.517 in 2006 and 24.240 in 2023, while Wānaka more than doubled from 5.043 in 2006 to 11.919 in 2023, joined by Cromwell (7,1k) and Alexandra (5,7k).

Across the northern South Island ("Top of the South"), three compact sunlit regions combined for 159.822 inhabitants in 2023 (3,2% of New Zealand): Tasman Region (9.858,3 km²) rose 69,9% from 34.026 in 1991 to 57.807 in 2023 (led by Richmond 18,4k and Motueka 8,2k); compact Nelson Region (904,6 km²) climbed from 36.456 to 52.584 (density 58,13 per km², second highest in New Zealand behind Auckland); and wine-exporting Marlborough Region (11.182,9 km²) expanded from 35.148 to 49.431, anchored by Blenheim (3,8k in 1911 to 28,8k in 2023) and ferry port Picton (4,7k). At the opposite extreme sit New Zealand's two demographic laggards. Southland Region (35.537,4 km²) shrank after 1986 freezing-works closures from 99.954 in 1991 to 93.339 in 2006 before dairy conversions restored it barely above its 1991 level at 100.143 in 2023 (2%; density 2,82 per km²), while port Bluff dropped from 3,3k in 1966 to 1,8k in 2023. Rain-drenched West Coast Region (29.974,8 km²) remained mainland New Zealand's sparsest province (31.563 in 1991, 31.320 in 2006 and 33.390 in 2023; 0,7%; density 1,11 per km²), with coal-and-timber port Greymouth still below its 1956 peak (8.948 against 8.331 in 2023) and Westport similarly down from 5.522 in 1956 to 4.479. Far to the east in the Pacific, the Chatham Islands Territory (2.595,8 km² buffered island mask) counted 633 usually resident inhabitants in 2023 (0,24 per km²), centred on the fishing and administrative settlement of Waitangi (210) [@aotearoa20242023].

## Metropolitan Concentration and the Modern Urban Hierarchy

Modern New Zealand exhibits one of the highest urban concentrations in the developed world, with over 85% of residents living in urban areas and over three fifths concentrated inside just six metropolitan labour markets [@alimi2019more; @whitehead2023comparison]. Figure \ref{fig:nz-hierarchy} displays the twelve largest catalogued centres and the log-log rank-size profile spanning all 547 settlements.

<figure class="crd-figure-block" id="fig:nz-hierarchy">
<img class="crd-figure-img" src="/artefacts/project_austral/1.0-modern-new-zealand/modern_new_zealand_urban_hierarchy.png" alt="fig:nz-hierarchy" loading="lazy" />
<figcaption class="crd-caption"><span class="crd-caption-label">Figure 3.</span> Twelve largest catalogued modern New Zealand settlements (Panel A) and rank-size distribution across 547 centres with upper-half power-law fit ($\alpha = 1,23$, $R^2 = 0,98$ across the top 180 settlements, Panel B), 1907 to 2025.</figcaption>
</figure>

In 2023, the six Official Functional Urban Areas—Auckland (1.622.925), Christchurch (510.801), Wellington (418.152), Hamilton (213.933), Tauranga (171.105) and Dunedin (124.839)—held 3.061.755 people, representing 61,3% of Aotearoa New Zealand. Auckland Metro alone outweighs Christchurch by 3,18 to 1 and Wellington by 3,88 to 1, inverting New Zealand's nineteenth-century four-centre balance (when 1911 Auckland 102,7k, Christchurch 80,2k, Wellington 70,7k and Dunedin 64,2k stood within a narrow band) into unmistakable northern metropolitan primacy [@pool2026peopling; @alimi2019more]. Across all 547 catalogued localities, the upper-tier rank-size regression (top 180 centres) yields a steep primate power law of $\alpha = 1,23$ ($R^2 = 0,98$; full 547-centre slope $-1,54$, $R^2 = 0,96$), tightening further to $\alpha = 1,28$ ($R^2 = 0,97$) when the 55 suburban commuter satellites are excluded. Table \ref{tab:region-shares} pairs each Regional Council's shifting national population share across 1991, 2006 and 2023 with its catalogued locality count and leading recorded settlement.

# Limitations

Four methodological and archival constraints qualify long-run demographic series for modern New Zealand between 1907 and 2026.

First, repeated subnational boundary reorganisations—from ten Provincial Districts (1907 to 1951) through thirteen Statistical Areas (1961 to 1976) and twenty-two Local Government Regions (1981 to 1986) to the sixteen post-1989 Regional Councils and 2010 unified Auckland Council—prevent exact cell-by-cell tracking of modern Regional Councils back to 1907 without areal interpolation [@dixon1989new; @statistics1962population]. In our constant-boundary benchmark matrix, pre-1991 Regional Council columns backcast 1991 shares proportionally to national census totals, masking the historical North Island drift; conversely, uniform areal disaggregation of the old eleven-province HGIS layer across 1910 to 1940 under-allocates compact Auckland Region on the early decadal raster slices prior to the 1955 Regional Council transition. Readers tracking inter-island shifts before 1989 should therefore rely directly on the primary provincial and statistical-area census tables.

Second, enumeration coverage and ethnic definitions shifted across the century. Early Dominion provincial tables separated Māori and non-Māori populations until 1951, late-century censuses transitioned from blood quantum to self-identified multi-response ethnicity [@didham2012effect; @kukutai2011contemporary], and the online-first 2018 Census suffered acute response drops among Māori and Pacific households requiring substantial administrative-data imputation [@kukutai2019census; @aotearoa20202018]. Although 2023 field collection improved direct coverage, Cyclone Gabrielle disrupted enumeration across East Coast communities [@aotearoa20242023], and the usually resident census base (4,99M in March 2023) sits roughly 4% to 6% below official mid-2025 Estimated Resident Population (~5,3M) because of net undercount adjustment and post-border-reopening migration [@crothers2021research].

Third, excluding all 67 Territorial Authority district aggregates from the 547-entry locality gazetteer prevents double counting of rural county populations, yet omits several mid-sized provincial cities whose official urban areas overlapped excluded Territorial Authority records (Whangārei, Gisborne, Napier, Hastings, New Plymouth, Palmerston North, Whanganui, Nelson, Timaru and Invercargill). Consequently, regional gazetteer leaders in Table \ref{tab:region-shares} for Gisborne (Manutūkē), Nelson (Rai Valley), Southland (Bluff) and Northland (Kerikeri) reflect the largest non-TA urban locality in the register rather than the omitted provincial city proper. Additionally, the historical borough table assigns a 1911 homonym figure (10.991) to Otago's small town of Palmerston (an early archival conflation with Palmerston North), which is documented transparently rather than silently altered.

Fourth, coarse coastal rasterisation creates two localised pixel-boundary offsets without affecting national or census totals: the buffered mask area (304.565,6 km²) exceeds subaerial HGIS land area (269.400 km²) by 13,1% across indented fiords, harbours and offshore islands, a 2020–2025 border-pixel exchange shifts roughly 31k raster inhabitants from tiny Nelson Region into adjoining Tasman while conserving their combined sum, and Chatham Islands' constant-boundary 1991/2006 placeholder (5.000) resolves to its true 633 census population at 2023.

# Conclusion

From Dominion proclamation in September 1907 to the mid-2020s, Aotearoa New Zealand transformed from a small pastoral outpost of barely one million mostly British-descended settlers into an intensely urbanised, multi-ethnic Pacific nation of 4,99M enumerated residents at the 2023 Census (5,1M on the 2025 raster; roughly 5,3M estimated resident population in 2025) [@pool2026peopling; @aotearoa20242023]. That nearly fivefold expansion absorbed severe First World War and 1918 influenza losses, surged through the post-war baby boom, weathered 1980s industrial restructuring and 2010–2011 Canterbury earthquake disruption and emerged from the COVID-19 pandemic with minimal excess mortality [@pool2007new; @blakely2008inequalities; @bryant2026estimating].

Three structural shifts define modern New Zealand's human geography. First, the century-long North Island drift lifted the northern island from 55,9% of non-Māori inhabitants in 1911 (62,3% total in 1921) to 76,3% (3,81M) in 2023, concentrating more than half the entire country inside the four upper North Island regions and one third (1,66M, 33,2%) inside unified Auckland Council alone [@jackson2019subnational; @alimi2019more]. Second, Māori demographic recovery and rapid post-1945 urbanisation—joined by Pacific family settlement and post-1987 skilled Asian migration—remade Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch into culturally plural metropolises even as ethnic mortality and health gaps remain an unfinished public-health challenge [@pool1991iwi; @spoonley2012welcome; @disney2017changing; @white2026decreasing]. Third, metropolitan concentration tightened into a steep primate urban hierarchy ($\alpha = 1,23$, $R^2 = 0,98$) in which six Functional Urban Areas hold 61,3% of all New Zealanders, leaving rural provinces and outer South Island districts to navigate rapid demographic ageing across the decades ahead [@jackson2019subnational; @whitehead2023comparison].

# Footnotes

All numerical values follow European decimal formatting (comma decimals and dot thousands separators) paired with semantic magnitude suffixes (k for thousands, M for millions). Constant-boundary regional benchmark tables retain the post-1989 sixteen Regional Councils plus the Chatham Islands Territory (including the 2010 unified Auckland Council limits), whereas primary Dominion enumerations (1911 to 1951) follow contemporary Provincial District boundaries and HGIS snapshots transition from eleven provincial units (1910 to 1950) to seventeen modern regional units (1960 to 2025). Census counts from 1921 onward include both Māori and non-Māori populations; the 1911 provincial breakdown reports non-Māori residents (1.008.468) prior to adding the separate Māori census roll (49.844).
